issues.description:
The access to `request.files['file']` became slower when I upgraded to Werkzeug 2.3. A 12.1 MB file used to take a couple of ms, but now it takes about 8 seconds.

```python
from werkzeug import Request, Response, run_simple

@Request.application
def app(request):
    if request.method == "POST":
        return Response(request.files["file"].filename)

    return Response("""<!doctype html>
<meta charset=utf-8>
<form method=post enctype=multipart/form-data>
<input type=file name=file>
<input type=submit>
</form>
""", mimetype="text/html")

run_simple("127.0.0.1", 5000, app)
```

Environment:

- Python version: 3.10
- Werkzeug version: 2.3.0

issues.summary: larger file content is prepended with CR LF
issues.description:
Starting with werkzeug version 2.3.0, posting payload content that is larger than 65575 bytes will result in two extra bytes prepended to the file content. Version 2.2.3 and earlier doesn't have this issue (meaning, in earlier versions the server prints the exact same thing in both cases, as expected).

In the test below I send two files. They're both identical with the only difference being that `file_a.txt` is 65428 bytes, while `file_b.txt` is 65429 (extra bytes in the request body are added by headers, multipart format etc.).

Test input files are attached.

Speculation: since it's close to 2**16 (65536), maybe it has something to do with that.

Client:
```
import requests

# This will print b'xxxxxxxxxx' on the server.
requests.post('http://127.0.0.1:9999/', files={'hello': open('file_a.txt')})

# This will print b'\r\nxxxxxxxxxx' on the server.
requests.post('http://127.0.0.1:9999/', files={'hello': open('file_b.txt')})
```

Server:
```
from flask import Flask, request
app = Flask(__name__)


@app.route('/', methods=['POST'])
def route():
    print(request.headers['content-length'])
    print(request.files['hello'].stream.read()[:10])
    return ''


if __name__ == '__main__':
    app.run(host='127.0.0.1', port=9999)
```
[file_a.txt](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/files/11359752/file_a.txt)
[file_b.txt](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/files/11359753/file_b.txt)


<!--
Describe the expected behavior that should have happened but didn't.
-->

Environment:

- Python version: 3.11 (but also saw the same behavior on 3.8)
- Werkzeug version: 2.3.2 (earliest one I could reproduce this in was 2.3.0)

issues.description:

```
import base64
from werkzeug.datastructures.auth import Authorization
token = base64.encodebytes(b"This has base64 padding").decode("utf-8").strip()

a.token
```

```
VGhpcyBoYXMgYmFzZTY0IHBhZGRpbmc=
```

issues.summary: calls to `iri_to_uri` fails when the argument is a bytestring
issues.description:
Calls to `iri_to_uri` fails when the argument is a bytestring. Here's an example:

```console
>>> from werkzeug import urls
>>> urls.iri_to_uri(b'/foo')
<stdin>:1: DeprecationWarning: Passing bytes is deprecated and will not be supported in Werkzeug 3.0.
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/midchildan/Documents/playground/werkzeug/lib/python3.10/site-packages/werkzeug/urls.py", line 983, in iri_to_uri
    iri = iri.decode(charset)
TypeError: decode() argument 'encoding' must be str, not None
```

This is what should've happened instead:

```console
>>> from werkzeug import urls
>>> urls.iri_to_uri(b'/foo')
>>> '/foo'
```

Environment:

- Python version: 3.10.11
- Werkzeug version: 2.3.4

#2654 added scrypt support, but couldn't make it the default because [PyPy didn't support it at the time](https://foss.heptapod.net/pypy/pypy/-/issues/3921). Now PyPy has fixed that and [made a release](https://doc.pypy.org/en/latest/release-v7.3.12.html), I'm comfortable with making scrypt the default.

The `__version__` attribute is an old pattern from early in Python packaging. Setuptools eventually made it easier to use the pattern by allowing reading the value from the attribute at build time, and some other build backends have done the same.

However, there's no reason to expose this directly in code anymore. It's usually easier to use feature detection (`hasattr`, `try/except`) instead. `importlib.metadata.version("werkzeug")` can be used to get the version at runtime in a standard way, if it's really needed.

This issue is in three parts:

### `no-transform` directive always returns None

This directive has no arguments (either in current RFC 9111 or older RFC 2616)

```python
from werkzeug.http import parse_cache_control_header

cc = parse_cache_control_header("no-transform")
print(f"{cc.no_transform=}")
```

Output: 
```
cc.no_transform=None
```

Expected: boolean based on presence

### `min-fresh` directive returns `"*"` if missing required argument

```python
from werkzeug.http import parse_cache_control_header

cc = parse_cache_control_header("min-fresh")
print(f"{cc.min_fresh=}")
```

Output:
```
cc.min_fresh='*'
```

Expected: `None` since the argument is required and `"*"` doesn't have a semantic meaning for this directive.

### type stubs are incorrect

- `no_cache` returns `str` not `bool`.
- `bool` properties never return `None`
- `max_stale` returns `"*"` in addition to `int`.
- `RequestCacheControl` immutability is not reflected.

Environment:

- Python version: N/A
- Werkzeug version: 3.0.2

issues.summary: watchdog: Prevent reload if a file gets closed without any changes
issues.description:
**What's the issue?**

[watchdog 5.0](https://github.com/gorakhargosh/watchdog/blob/master/changelog.rst#500) introduced a [new signal that is fired when a file gets closed without any changes written](https://github.com/gorakhargosh/watchdog/pull/1059).  
This leads to random reloads when something opens and closes a file. `opened` events are already ignored, so we should ignore the new `closed_no_write` events too.

**How to reproduce?**

Update to watchdog 5.0+ and wait for the reloads to come in.

**What's the expected behavior?**

Werkzeug should only reload if there are actual changes to the code base.

**Environment**

- Python version: 3.11.2
- Werkzeug version: 3.0.4
- watchdog version: 5.0.2

`OrderedMultiDict` is not used by Werkzeug. issues.summary: werkzeug misdecodes multipart line breaks if 64kb chunk ends in the middle of final CR+LF
issues.description:
The following minimalist flask application and upload code causes a wrongly decoded multipart payload to be saved. The application file `upload.py`  and test case `testcase` are in the attached zip file [reproducer.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/23521331/reproducer.zip).

 - run application: `mkdir upload ; python3 -m flask --app upload.py run -p 32269`
 - upload the test case (from a separate shell, of course): `netcat 127.0.0.1 32269 < testcase`

Behold the fact that the testcase ends in:
```
000100f0: 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000  ................
00010100: 0000 0000 0000 000d 0a2d 2d30 3633 6166  .........--063af
00010110: 6334 6362 6534 3661 3734 3035 3930 3938  c4cbe46a74059098
00010120: 3831 3433 3937 3165 3262 642d 2d0d 0a    8143971e2bd--..
```

whereby the *payload* should end with a bunch of zeros.

What happens is that the downloaded file has a stray `\x0d` at the end, leading to a file of length 65432 bytes, while the correct length should be 65431 bytes:
```
0000ff80: 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000  ................
0000ff90: 0000 0000 0000 000d                      ........
```

My understanding of the cause is that the code [here](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/main/src/werkzeug/formparser.py#L368-L370) splits the input in chunks of size 65536. Its state machine is updated by what it sees. If the chunk is broken in the middle of the final line break (which is precisely what happens here), the [quite tolerant regexp here](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/main/src/werkzeug/sansio/multipart.py#L63-L65) will recognize a single `\n` as a legitimate line break marker, and thus let `\r` be part of the payload.

```
'3.1.3'
```

issues.description:
If `server_name` is passed to `Map.bind_from_environ`, and a `subdomain` is not passed in (as usually it's not possible to know it), it will try to detect the subdomain by removing `server_name` as a suffix from `host`. This restricts routing to only the configured `server_name`, even if we don't have any subdomain-based routing rules.

Move Flask's `subdomain_matching` param into `Map` (where `host_matching` is already). `bind_to_environ` should not extract a subdomain unless it's enabled.

`Map.bind_to_environ` can be passed an environ or a request object. But it always calls `get_host(environ)`. If it used `request.host` if a request was passed, this would check `request.trusted_hosts` during routing. See pallets/flask#5636

Werkzeug often reloads slowly when in `watchdog` mode for me. It can take 10 to 20 seconds before changes are noticed. This may be due to having a lot of `extra_files` being watched, I have ~110 extra files listed.

With `stat` reload mode the reload happens almost immediately.

Environment:

- Linux (`watchdog` uses `inotify`)
- Python version: 3.12.6
- Werkzeug version: 3.1.3


I did some testing and it appears that the `WatchdogReloaderLoop.EventHandler` in `_reloader.py` is a bit slow due to unnecessary pattern matching. This 
```
        class EventHandler(PatternMatchingEventHandler):
            def on_any_event(self, event: FileModifiedEvent):  # type: ignore
                if event.event_type not in {
                   EVENT_TYPE_CLOSED,
                   EVENT_TYPE_CREATED,
                   EVENT_TYPE_DELETED,
                   EVENT_TYPE_MODIFIED,
                   EVENT_TYPE_MOVED,
                }:
                   # skip events that don't involve changes to the file
                   return

                trigger_reload(event.src_path)
```
becomes much faster if irrelevant event types are discarded before pattern matching in `dispatch`:
```
        class EventHandler(PatternMatchingEventHandler):
            def dispatch(self, event: FileSystemEvent) -> None:
                if event.event_type not in {
                   EVENT_TYPE_CLOSED,
                   EVENT_TYPE_CREATED,
                   EVENT_TYPE_DELETED,
                   EVENT_TYPE_MODIFIED,
                   EVENT_TYPE_MOVED,
                }:
                   # skip events that don't involve changes to the file
                   return

                super().dispatch(event)

            def on_any_event(self, event: FileModifiedEvent):  # type: ignore
                trigger_reload(event.src_path)
```
This actually fixes the slowness issue for me and reloads are instant.

I have a pretty complex terminal prompt (doing git and python virtualenv stuff) that causes ~300 events to be sent to the dispatch method. Previously, holding enter in my terminal for a second would cause 100% core usage for 10 seconds in the dev server. With the changed version, core usage stays below 50% even if I hold enter indefinitely.

issues.summary: duplicate rule check needs to consider more
issues.description:
The duplicate rule check added in #3038 isn't exact enough. It doesn't account for methods. It can't check equality `self.methods == other.methods`, it needs to check intersection `self.method & other.methods` since _any_ shared method would result in a duplicate. I don't think that's appropriate for `__eq__` though, as it's not exactly equality and `==` is used elsewhere. Also not sure if `strict_slashes` and `merge_slashes` is being accounted for. @pgjones 

While looking at `Rule.methods` I noticed that it can be `None` instead of a set of values. Why is this? Checks for that are throughout the code, and I also can't find logic saying the default is `GET` in that case. What's going on with that?

issues.summary: Response.make_conditional(..., accept_ranges=True) does not send Accept-Ranges header early enough
issues.description:
#1711 refactored the `_process_range_request` method. Before, it used to set `Accept-Ranges` as the first thing it did. Now, it only sets `Accept-Ranges` when sending a response to a Range request, which defeats the point of that header (which is to advertise support for range requests, so it's not useful if the client is already doing a range request).

basic repro:
```py
# /// script
# dependencies = [
#     "werkzeug==3.1.5",
# ]
# ///
from werkzeug.wrappers import Request, Response
from werkzeug.serving import run_simple
from werkzeug.wsgi import wrap_file
import io

def application(environ, start_response):
    text = b"Hello world!"
    wrap = wrap_file(environ, io.BytesIO(text))
    response = Response(wrap, mimetype='text/plain')
    response.set_etag('test')
    response.make_conditional(environ, accept_ranges=True, complete_length=len(text))
    return response(environ, start_response)


run_simple('127.0.0.1', 5000, application)
```

when making a request against this with `curl -i http://127.0.0.1:5000/`, there is no Accept-Ranges header. It only appears when doing a range request like `curl -i http://127.0.0.1:5000/ -H "Range: bytes=0-7"`. Note that when changing the version constraint to `werkzeug<1.0` (before #1711 was merged), we do see Accept-Ranges in the response to the basic request.

The fix would be to move the setting of Accept-Ranges back to the very beginning of `_process_range_request`.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.13.12
- Werkzeug version: 3.1.5

issues.summary: WSGIRequestHandler sends 100 Continue twice when client sends Expect: 100-continue
issues.description:
`WSGIRequestHandler` sends `HTTP/1.1 100 Continue` twice when a client includes the `Expect: 100-continue` header. Python's `BaseHTTPRequestHandler.parse_request()` calls `handle_expect_100()` which sends the first response. Then `run_wsgi()` ([serving.py L313-314](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/main/src/werkzeug/serving.py#L313-L314)) independently checks the same header and writes a second one. Neither layer clears the header after acting on it.

HTTP clients that strictly parse interim responses — notably the AWS SDK's Netty-based async client — treat the second `100 Continue` as the start of the final response, causing all uploads to fail with status code 100.

```python
import socket
import threading
from werkzeug.serving import make_server


def app(environ, start_response):
    # Read and discard request body
    environ["wsgi.input"].read()
    start_response("200 OK", [("Content-Type", "text/plain")])
    return [b"ok"]


server = make_server("127.0.0.1", 9876, app, threaded=True)
thread = threading.Thread(target=server.handle_request)
thread.start()

sock = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 9876))
sock.sendall(
    b"PUT /test HTTP/1.1\r\n"
    b"Host: 127.0.0.1:9876\r\n"
    b"Content-Length: 5\r\n"
    b"Expect: 100-continue\r\n"
    b"\r\n"
)

# Collect the full response before sending the body
import time
time.sleep(0.5)
response = sock.recv(4096)
print(response.decode())

sock.sendall(b"hello")
time.sleep(0.5)
response = sock.recv(4096)
print(response.decode())

sock.close()
thread.join()
server.server_close()

```

**Expected:** One `HTTP/1.1 100 Continue` response, followed by the final `200 OK` after the body is sent.

**Actual:** Two `HTTP/1.1 100 Continue` responses are sent before the final `200 OK`. Raw output:

```
HTTP/1.1 100 Continue

HTTP/1.1 100 Continue

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
...
```

A minimal fix would be to override `handle_expect_100` to suppress the stdlib's response, since `run_wsgi()` already handles it:

```python
def handle_expect_100(self) -> bool:
    return True
```

Environment:

- Python version: 3.12
- Werkzeug version: 3.1.7 (main branch)

#3113 updated `get_host` to always validate the host characters. However, it also disallowed the empty string. This is a bit too strict, it should only _validate_ the string if it's not empty, or if `trusted_hosts` is passed. And if it's not valid characters, it should return the empty string rather than failing.

This will match Django's behavior. I thought I had matched it before, as I referred to it when trying to figure out the right behavior here. But I ended up being more strict than it is. It treats empty strings and invalid characters as the empty string, rather than immediately returning an error.

`Host` is also nonexistant in HTTP/0.9 and optional in HTTP/1.0, so it might appear as the empty string in those cases and should be passed through.

To be clear: domain names still can't contain `_` or a bunch of other characters. If you have a domain like that, you need to report it to/fix whatever's generating such a name. It just shouldn't fail loudly immediately, although it might produce invalid results or fail in other ways later.

issues.summary: FloatConverter breaks for values smaller than 0.0001
issues.description:
`FloatConverter` uses scientific notation (`1e-05`) when building URLs with values smaller than 0.0001. This leads to URLs, that can not be resolved, as `FloatConverter` does not handle values containing letters (regex: `\d+\.\d+`).

The following listing illustrates the issue:

```python
from werkzeug.routing import Map, Rule
from werkzeug.routing.converters import FloatConverter
import typing as t

map = Map([
    Rule('/<float:x>', endpoint='foo'),
])
mapAdapter = map.bind('bar')

print(url := mapAdapter.build('foo', values={'x': 1}), mapAdapter.test(url))
print(url := mapAdapter.build('foo', values={'x': 0.00001}), mapAdapter.test(url))
print(url := '/0.00001', mapAdapter.test(url))
```

This leads to the following output:

```
/1.0 True
/1e-05 False
/0.00001 True
```

In the second row, the generated URL can not be resolved. 

There are multiple ways to fix this issue.  One could for example adjust the regex to handle these cases (`\d+\.\d+(e[+-]/d+)?` instead of `\d+\.\d+`). Another option would be to suppress scientific notation when building URLs:

```python
class FixedFloatConverter(FloatConverter):
    def to_url(self, value: t.Any) -> str:
        return f'{self.num_convert(value):f}'
    
map = Map([
    Rule('/<ffloat:x>', endpoint='foo'),
], converters={'ffloat': FixedFloatConverter})
mapAdapter = map.bind('bar')

print(url := mapAdapter.build('foo', values={'x': 1}), mapAdapter.test(url))
print(url := mapAdapter.build('foo', values={'x': 0.00001}), mapAdapter.test(url))
print(url := '/0.00001', mapAdapter.test(url))
```

This produces the desired result:

```
/1.000000 True
/0.000010 True
/0.00001 True
```

Environment:

- Python version: not relevant
- Werkzeug version: 3.1.7

issues.summary: Add Client.query() test shortcut for the QUERY HTTP method (RFC 10008)
issues.description:
The HTTP `QUERY` method was standardized in
[RFC 10008](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc10008/) (June 2026): a safe,
idempotent request method that carries content in the request body.

Werkzeug's test `Client` has shortcuts for
`get`/`post`/`put`/`delete`/`patch`/`options`/`head`/`trace`, but not `query`.
I'd like to add `Client.query()` to mirror the others.

---

Is this solvable without changes to Werkzeug? Yes — `client.open("/x",
method="QUERY")` already works, and routing plus body parsing already handle
`QUERY` (form parsing is mimetype-driven, not method-gated). This is purely the
missing test-client shortcut, added for consistency with the other methods.

I have a branch ready with the change, a test, and a changelog entry, and am
happy to open a PR if this sounds good.

This is a more conservative version of #3237 that only fixes bugs/unintended behavior and otherwise doesn't break existing URLs. I'll target this at 3.2 since it does change what's accept a bit still.

- Non-ASCII digits are accepted.
- `int(fixed_digits=4, signed=True)` counts the negative sign as a digit.
- `float` overflow values (too large to fit in float) become `inf`, which is a special, unexpected value that can cause problems when used later on.
  - Underflow values become `0.0`, which is a "normal" value.
  - Binary float cannot represent all values, but that's a very abstract concept for users to understand and ensure in URLs.
- #3147 prevented scientific notation by limiting to 6 decimal places, which excludes many legitimate values.

A 1-to-1 mapping of URLs to parsed values is not a goal. This will be documented for these converters. However, `.4` and `4.` will remain disallowed, I want to keep the more obvious `left.right` syntax only. And `4.` would cause issues with Markdown URL detection.

The private `NumberConverter` base seems to be more trouble than the small amount of duplication it removes, especially if we also tried to extend it to `decimal` later, so I'll remove it.

This was disabled by default in 2.1 in 2022. There doesn't seem to be any reason to produce absolute redirect URLs now. The only issue reported, in 2023, was it had previously obscured an open redirect bug in another library, and that should have been addressed at the browser level as well.

Code search shows exactly three uses of setting it to `True` https://sourcegraph.com/search?q=context:global+lang:Python+%22autocorrect_location_header+%3D+True%22+-file:site-packages/+-file:werkzeug/+-file:flask/+-repo:%5Egithub%5C.com/pallets/werkzeug%24+&patternType=keyword&sm=0 Two of them have no apparent use, the third is a temporary workaround related to the issue mentioned above. Searching for only `autocorrect_location_header` shows that every other use is setting it to `False`. If it's truly needed, `response.location = url_for(..., _external=True)` or `urljoin(request.host, response.location)` will do it explicitly.

A side note, `Response.autocorrect_location_header` doesn't know about `trusted_hosts`, so it will use whatever `Host` is sent. This doesn't actually mean anything in practice, since it only affects the requests you make, and your browser or code would be sending a trusted `Host` header.

User agent parsing was removed in 2.0 in 2021 in #2078. The intention was that `Request.user_agent_class` could be set to a subclass of `UserAgent` that parsed and populated the other properties. The full string could be accessed with `request.user_agent.string`.

This never seems to have been adopted. There are no meaningful results in https://sourcegraph.com/search?q=context:global+lang:Python+%22user_agent_class%22+-file:site-packages/+-file:werkzeug/+-file:flask/+-repo:%5Egithub%5C.com/pallets/werkzeug%24+&patternType=keyword&sm=0 (and half of those are unrelated to Werkzeug). Searching for "werkzeug user agent" or "werkzeug user_agent_class" on search engines or PyPI brings up nothing.

This isn't particularly good for type checking, as `Request` would need to be generic on `user_agent_class` in order for a subclass to expose more properties. It saves approximately one line over parsing the user agent string directly, and requires implementing an interface that might not fit what you need anyway.

Deprecate this and make `Request.user_agent` a string. `UserAgent` can subclass `str` during the deprecation, and warn when accessing `user_agent.string`.

- `input_stream` is explicitly documented as unsafe compared to its wrapped counterpart in `stream`.
- `remote_user` is only mentioned in passing as part of CGI that WSGI accepts for compatibility.
- `is_multithread`, `is_multiprocess`, and `is_run_once` are about how the server is running workers. But I can't think of how that matters to the application, code must avoid globals and use external storage regardless of the worker type.
- All of these can be accessed directly from `request.environ` if needed, they even still have their correct types.
- I can't find any uses of `environ_property` (or `header_property`) in external code.
- None of the many other WSGI and CGI keys are exposed.
- ASGI has no concept of any of these.

It currently checks `text/html or accept_xhtml`. But HTML is not valid XHTML (or XML in general), so responding true if `application/xml` is asked for is wrong. It should only check `text/html`.

`accept_xhtml` should also be deprecated, XHTML is not something anyone's seeking out to use nowadays https://w3techs.com/technologies/details/ml-xhtml_any. I would be extremely surprised if any client was _requesting_ XHTML in `Accept`, or at least requesting it without also requesting HTML. Additionally, XHTML as used in practice is valid HTML, and it's unlikely an app would have a way to produce XHTML _or_ HTML based on the `Accept` header. And if they really need it, the app can still use `application/xhtml+xml in accept`.

While looking at #3284, I noticed this. This is incorrect, `SERVER_NAME` and `SERVER_PORT` refer to the local WSGI server. They're used as a fallback if the `Host` header isn't set, but that definitely will be set due to the `X-Forwarded-Host` header.

issues.summary: `Request.application` doesn't type check when decorating a method
issues.description: `Request.application` supports decorating a function or a method. However, it's type annotation only accounts for a function. Needs to have overloads to support both.
It's a less powerful version of `Request.application`.

The `Request` `populate_request` argument adds `environ["werkzeug.request"] = self` on init. This isn't used anywhere.

- It's documented as being potentially useful for debugging, with no explanation how. With #3281, the goal is to pass around the request instead of the environ, then this won't be needed at all.
- It creates a reference loop, `environ` holds a reference to `request`, which holds a reference in `request.environ`. This is handled by the garbage collector, but it's not great.
- It's not guaranteed that `environ is environ["werkzeug.request"].environ`. For example, the test client copies the environ to isolate any changes the app makes, but doesn't update the cached request. Any middleware that didn't know about Werkzeug could result in the same thing.
- Any middleware that modifies the environ can result in the request having stale data either through init or cached properties.

I can't think of an easy way to deprecate the `werkzeug.request` key. Given that it's essentially undocumented and not used anywhere, I'm guessing that just removing it in 4.0 will be fine.

It seems to be a less efficient way to iterate over a file rather than just iterating over it directly. It's only yielding 8 kB chunks at a time. The intention of `wsgi.file_wrapper` in WSGI is to expose more efficient file sending from the operating system. The key is optional, our `wrap_file` function is allowed to return the file unchanged if it's not set.

They currently store strings, then call `iri_to_uri` in `get_wsgi_headers`. And that's only done for WSGI, so sans-IO/ASGI doesn't get it. Instead, they should always be stored as URIs, and accessed as IRIs.

No other headers are "fixed" in `get_wsgi_headers`. `Response.headers` is considered "raw" values, where it's the responsibility of the code setting it to set a valid value. That's what the properties provide: set a Python value, get the right encoded header value.

issues.summary: dev server doesn't close response iterable when client resets connection
issues.description:
If the client resets the connection while the dev server is sending a response, the response iterable's `close()` is never called. With `send_file` this leaves the file open, and you get `ResourceWarning: unclosed file` later. Under `pytest -W error` that fails an unrelated test. I see it in browser tests when a page closes while an asset is still downloading.

```python
import socket
import struct
import threading
import time

from werkzeug.serving import make_server


class Body:
    def __iter__(self):
        for _ in range(1000):
            yield b"x" * 65536

    def close(self):
        print("closed")


def app(environ, start_response):
    start_response("200 OK", [("Content-Type", "text/plain")])
    return Body()


server = make_server("127.0.0.1", 0, app)
threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

sock = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", server.port))
sock.sendall(b"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\n\r\n")
sock.recv(4096)
# close with RST instead of FIN
sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_LINGER, struct.pack("ii", 1, 0))
sock.close()
time.sleep(1)
server.shutdown()
```

Expected: `closed` is printed.

Actual: nothing is printed (10 of 10 runs).

Cause: `write()` fails with the reset, then the `finally` block in `run_wsgi` drains the socket before closing the iterable. The socket is readable because of the reset, so `self.rfile.read(10_000_000)` raises `ConnectionResetError`, which skips `selector.close()` and `application_iter.close()`.

https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/85dd69bda8f7591089ded638b67d57cf496676fb/src/werkzeug/serving.py#L343-L371

Catching `OSError` around that read and breaking out of the loop fixes it. I have that change with a test, and can open a PR against `stable` if that works for you.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.12.10 (macOS arm64)
- Werkzeug version: 3.1.9 (same code on `main`)

Watchdog version is not pinned to v6 so now that v7 has been released reloader gets broken.

I think the issue comes from this breaking change:
> [core] Changed pattern matching mechanism from using path.match() to path.full_match(). Users must update patterns to glob-like syntax: e.g., *.py to **/*.py.

Changelog reference: https://github.com/gorakhargosh/watchdog/blob/master/changelog.rst#700


Replicate:
1. Install `werkzeug[watchdog]==3.1.9`
2. Run `run_simple("127.0.0.1", 5000, app, use_reloader=True, reloader_type="watchdog")`
3. Update a .py file
4. With watchdog v6 this is where you see reloader note in the logs, but with v7 there is nothing


Expected behavior:
I expect reloader to work on `.py` file change but it doesn't work with watchdog 7.x.


Environment:

- Python version: 3.14
- Werkzeug version: 3.1.9


---

The quickest solution is to pin watchdog to `<7` to stop it from braking on new installations.
That is obviously not future proof so next step would be the code update to `patterns=["**/*.py", "**/*.pyc", "**/*.zip"]` and pin watchdog to `>=7`.But I think that might be a braking change for werkzeug because of `extra_files` and `exclude_patterns` which I have no idea how they work.
